analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent the repeal of the federal estate tax on large inherited fortunes.
analysis.headline: The estate tax repeal bill drew 22 Republican sponsors in the House but died in committee without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2001 Bush tax law had phased out the estate tax, but that repeal was scheduled to expire after 2010, bringing the tax back. This bill would have made the repeal permanent, meaning estates of any size would never owe federal estate tax again. The estate tax applies only to the largest inherited fortunes; in 2009 it reached estates above $3.5 million per person ($7 million per couple), and the highest rate that year was 45% on the amount above the exemption. The bill was referred to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee, where it received no hearing, no markup, and no vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the very largest estates — roughly the wealthiest quarter of one percent of families — would save the full value of the tax, which falls entirely on inheritances above a multi-million-dollar exemption. Families below that threshold already owed nothing, so they would see no change. The Treasury would lose the revenue, shifting the burden of funding the government to other taxpayers or borrowing.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes permanent the 2001 tax law's repeal of the estate tax and its gift-tax reductions, so the tax would never return after its scheduled 2010 lapse. [S2] [S3]

Under the 2009 law the estate tax exempted the first $3.5 million of an estate ($7 million per married couple) and taxed amounts above that at up to 45%, so repeal's savings go only to the largest inheritances. (General knowledge of the 2009 estate tax parameters the bill would eliminate.)
The bill makes permanent the repeal of the estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax, keeping the tax from returning in 2011.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The estate tax raises tens of billions of dollars a year almost entirely from very large estates; eliminating it permanently means that revenue must be replaced by other taxes, higher deficits, or lower spending. The tax itself touches so few families that no ordinary family would write a check because of this bill — the cost is the lost revenue, and estate-tax compliance obligations for estates under the exemption (a filing burden for some mid-size estates) would be removed.
analysis.who_pays_short: General federal taxpayers and the Treasury

drawbacks.text: Repeal permanently removes a highly progressive revenue source that falls only on the largest inherited fortunes, adding roughly tens of billions of dollars a year to deficits or requiring higher taxes elsewhere. (General knowledge of the tax's revenue base.)

Repealing the estate tax also removes the generation-skipping transfer tax, which prevents fortunes from skipping a generation's tax entirely through certain trusts — a provision aimed at the wealthiest families. [S2]

An honest supporter would acknowledge that repeal primarily benefits a small number of the largest family estates and businesses, and that the case for it rests on arguments about double taxation of saved income rather than any benefit to most families.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit is real but extremely narrow: a tax cut exclusively for heirs to fortunes above roughly $3.5 million per person, worth the most to the largest estates. The cost is spread across everyone else through lost federal revenue — tens of billions of dollars annually once fully phased in. For most families the trade is straightforwardly negative, and the bill's design (permanent repeal with no revenue offset) makes the fiscal cost larger than alternatives such as raising the exemption.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means Committee and never came back — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, and the Congress ended with the bill dead.

narrative.text: Representative Joseph Pitts introduced the bill on April 2, 2009, with 11 original cosponsors. [S1] [S3]
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which writes tax legislation. [S1] [S5]
Twenty-one House Republicans cosponsored the bill; every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican. [S4]

The complete action history shows only the introduction and the committee referral — the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or any vote, and it died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011. [S5]
The bill would have made the 2001 tax law's estate tax repeal permanent rather than letting it expire. [S2]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury and taxpayers generally kept a revenue source paid almost entirely by the largest estates. Wealthy families and estate-planning professionals did not get the permanent repeal they sought, though the tax's one-year full repeal in 2010 still occurred under existing law. (General knowledge of the 2010 lapse and its extension.)

sides.party_line_note: All 22 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans; the bill received no Democratic support and died in a committee chaired by a Democrat.

industries.industry: Heirs to the largest estates and wealthy families
industries.note: Permanent repeal would have saved the biggest inheritances the entire estate tax, with the revenue gap passed to other taxpayers. The benefit flows to the top sliver of households at the general public's expense.

Repeal would eliminate a major line of estate-tax and trust-planning business, though permanent repeal's certainty has its own planning value. If it had passed, wealthy clients and their advisors would both have gained a simpler, tax-free transfer.
